title: Who knowingly shares false political information online?
screen_reason: National US survey (n = 2,001, May-June 2022) whose headline descriptive result is the share of respondents agreeing they share political information on social media they believe may be false: 14%. That is a self-reported share of respondents who say they shared misinformation, with a stated denominator -> RECALL (sharing). It is reported behaviour, not a hypothetical or experimental sharing intention, so the exclusion for intentions does not apply. Everything else in the paper is correlational psychology.

estimates.platform: Social media, unspecified (the item says only 'on social media'; separate media-use items covered YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, blogs, Reddit, Truth Social, Telegram and 8Kun, but those are not part of this measure)
estimates.measure_type: % of US adults who agree or strongly agree that they share political information on social media even though they believe it may be false
estimates.value_raw: 14% of respondents agreed or strongly agreed (N = 2,001)
estimates.denominator: 2,001 US adults (900 male, 1,101 female; mean age 48.5; 43.58% with a bachelor's degree or higher) recruited through Qualtrics with the Cint and Dynata panels, quota-matched to US Census records on self-reported sex, age, race, education and income
estimates.definition: Selected 'agree' or 'strongly agree' on a 5-point Likert item; 'neither agree nor disagree' was grouped with disagreement as 'No' in Figure 1
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation - information that is false or misleading according to the best currently established knowledge (Ecker et al., 2021; Vraga & Bode, 2020) - is often spread unintentionally, [whereas] disinformation, a subcategory of misinformation, is spread with the deliberate intent to deceive". The survey item itself leaves falsity to the respondent: information 'I believe it may be false'.
estimates.source_quote: Though most participants disagreed with this statement, a non-trivial percentage of respondents (14%) indicated that they do intentionally share false political information on social media (Figure 1).
estimates.page_loc: Findings, Finding 1, p. 5; also the abstract and Essay summary ('we asked respondents if they share political information on social media that they believe is false; 14% indicated that they do')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Entirely self-reported and respondent-defined ('information ... I believe it may be false'); no external verification of anything the respondent actually shared. The authors offer convergent-validity evidence: the item correlates r = .53 with 'Just for kicks, I've said mean things to people on social media', r = .43 with 'I tend to manipulate others to get my way' and r = .35 with 'I have used deceit or lied to get my way', and its 14% aligns with published rates for admitted lying (14.1%) and persuasive bullshitting (17.3%).
estimates.moderator_quote: Our dependent variable asked respondents to rate their agreement with the following statement using a 5-point Likert-type scale (Figure 1): "I share information on social media about politics even though I believe it may be false."
estimates.notes: CRITICAL SCOPE LIMIT: this is KNOWING sharing only. Respondents who share political misinformation without realising it are not in the numerator, so 14% is not the share of Americans who shared misinformation - it is the share who admit doing so deliberately, and the paper's whole framing rests on that distinction. It is therefore not comparable with behavioural sharing prevalences, and the authors themselves expect it to be under-reported ('some of the spreaders of it in our sample could have denied it'). THRESHOLD: 'agree or strongly agree' on a 5-point scale, with the midpoint counted as No. platform_norm coded 'survey' because the item names no platform; where a self-report item enumerates specific platforms I code multi_platform instead. Note the paper over-reaches slightly in calling this '14% of the U.S. adult population' - it is 14% of a quota-matched opt-in online panel sample.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The comparison rates the paper cites - Serota and Levine's 14.1% admitting at least one 'big lie' per day, and Littrell et al.'s 17.3% admitting regular 'persuasive bullshitting' - are figures the paper takes from elsewhere, which R8 forbids keeping. (2) Figure 1 shows the full five-point distribution but the text gives only the collapsed 14%; no per-category percentages appear in the text or appendix, so no stricter variant (e.g. 'strongly agree' only) can be extracted. (3) Every other result is a correlation or regression coefficient, not a share: political behaviours (political violence r = .46, civil disobedience r = .44, protests r = .40, desire to run for office r = .52), feeling-thermometer ratings (QAnon r = .45, Proud Boys r = .42, White Nationalists r = .42, Putin r = .40), psychological predictors (need for chaos and dark tetrad both beta = .18), and media-source use (alternative social media r = .46, Truth Social/Telegram/8Kun r = .41 each). None carries a misinformation denominator. (4) The appendix reports agree/strongly-agree percentages for many scale items (e.g. sadism 'Just for kicks, I've said mean things on social media' 18.05%), but these measure personality, not misinformation sharing. (5) The essay summary's claim that 'only a small number of people are responsible for sharing most of it' is a CONCENTRATION statement attributed to previous studies, not a finding of this paper, and carries no conc_group_pct/conc_share_pct pair, so R1 rules it out. (6) The media-source analyses use N = 1,990 rather than 2,001 with no explanation.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey of 2,001 American adults, 26 May to 30 June 2022, fielded on Qualtrics with Cint and Dynata research panels and quota-matched to US Census records on self-reported sex, age, race, education and income (900 male, 1,101 female; mean age 48.54, SD 18.51; 43.58% bachelor's degree or higher). Both panel vendors comply with ESOMAR privacy standards; respondents were paid in vendor-redeemable incentives. Quality control: responses removed for failing six attention-check items or completing in under half the estimated median completion time of 18.6 minutes (estimated from a soft launch of n = 50). NO RESPONSE OR COOPERATION RATE IS REPORTED - this is an opt-in panel quota sample, not a probability sample, so the 'demographically representative' description is quota matching only. The prevalence measure is a single 5-point Likert self-report item, so no coding procedure and no inter-rater reliability apply; the authors instead argue for the item's validity from its correlations with sadism and Machiavellianism items (r = .35 to .53) and from convergence with published lying/bullshitting rates. They explicitly acknowledge two threats to the estimate: under-reporting by actual spreaders, and insincere agreement given to signal group identity or as a joke (citing Lopez & Hillygus, Schaffner & Luks, Smallpage et al.). Data came from a larger survey, so item-order and context effects cannot be assessed. Analyses: bivariate Pearson correlations, a principal components analysis of 17 media sources, and an OLS multiple regression (adjusted R2 = .44), with full tables in the appendix; the media-source analyses use N = 1,990 without explanation of the 11 dropped cases.
